Consume
kŏn-sūm´
v. (to destroy or use up entirely; rendering Hebrew kalah, 'akal, Greek analisko, dapanao)
From Latin consumo, to take up wholly. Scripture's consuming is chiefly God's: a fire that is His own nature, before which His people are preserved and against which nothing unholy stands.

Biblical Definition

To consume is to use up entirely, leaving nothing, and Scripture's primary use makes the consuming a divine attribute rather than a divine mood: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29). The words are quoted out of Deuteronomy into a passage about a kingdom which cannot be moved, so that the fire is set beside grace rather than against it. Precisely because that is what God is, the preservation of sinners requires an explanation, and Scripture gives two. The first is mercy: “It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not” (Lamentations 3:22). The prophet is sitting in the ruins of Jerusalem when he says it, which is the strongest possible setting for the claim. The second is immutability: “For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed” (Malachi 3:6). The people's survival rests on God's unchangeableness, not on their improvement. The word turns downward when men do the consuming, and James names the misuse exactly: “Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts” (James 4:3). Prayer offered so that appetite may be fed is prayer aimed at consumption.

Webster 1828 Definition

To destroy by separating the parts; to burn up; to waste; to spend or use entirely. Scripture calls God a consuming fire, grounds His people's survival in His mercy and immutability, and warns of prayers offered only to feed appetite.

expand to see more

CONSUME, v.t. [L. consumo; con and sumo, to take.] To destroy by separating the parts of a thing, by decomposition, as by fire, or eating; to burn up; to devour.

2. To waste; to squander; to spend; as, to consume an estate.

3. To spend; to cause to pass away, as time; as, to consume the day in idleness.

4. To destroy; to bring to utter ruin; to exterminate.

CONSUME, v.i. To waste away slowly; to be exhausted; to perish; as, the body consumes by sickness.

CONSUMING, ppr. Burning up; wasting; destroying; expending.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 12:29 — "For our God is a consuming fire."

Lamentations 3:22 — "It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not."

Malachi 3:6 — "For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed."

James 4:3 — "Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts."

Modern Corruption

The consuming fire has been enlisted for annihilationism — the claim that the lost are burned out of existence — and, in the opposite direction, softened until God's holiness threatens nothing at all.

expand to see more

Annihilationism takes the language of consuming and destruction as proof that the punishment of the wicked ends in extinction rather than in conscious suffering. The argument cannot carry the texts. Our Lord uses the same breath for the life and the punishment, everlasting in both directions (Matthew 25:46), and Revelation describes torment that ascends for ever and ever. Hebrews 12:29 is not describing the fate of the lost at all; it is a motive for reverence addressed to the church that receives an unshakable kingdom. The doctrine of eternal conscious punishment is the historic Christian position, and the confessions state it because Scripture does.

The commoner error runs the other way, keeping the word and removing its edge, so that God's holiness is a warmth rather than a fire and no one need serve Him with reverence and godly fear. Lamentations 3:22 loses everything under that treatment. If nothing was ever owed, mercy is not mercy, and Jeremiah's wonder in the ruins is sentimentality. Hold both together as Scripture does: God is a consuming fire; His people are not consumed; and the reason lies in His compassions and His unchangeableness, never in the diminishing of the fire.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kalah (to complete, finish, consume) and 'akal (to eat, devour) supply the Old Testament sense; Greek analisko (to use up) and dapanao (to spend, consume) render the wasting and the spending.

expand to see more

Hebrew kalah (H3615) — to complete, to finish, to consume; the verb of Lamentations 3:22 and Malachi 3:6.

Hebrew 'akal (H398) — to eat, to devour; used of fire eating up what it burns.

Hebrew 'esh (H784) — fire; the element in which the LORD appeared at Sinai and which Hebrews applies to His nature.

Greek katanalisko (G2654) — to consume utterly; the participle in “a consuming fire” at Hebrews 12:29.

Greek dapanao (G1159) — to spend, to consume; the verb of James 4:3 for spending an answer upon lusts.

Usage

"“Our God is a consuming fire” — the fire is what God is, not merely what He does when provoked."

"“It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed” — survival is credited to compassion, not to merit."

"“That ye may consume it upon your lusts” — prayer aimed at appetite is prayer amiss."
